script.title: Why a Doctor Injected Himself With Sick Blood

lines: A doctor injected himself with blood from pellagra patients.
His wife and his assistant did it too.
Pellagra was a painful skin disease sweeping the American South.
By 1912, South Carolina alone had 30,000 cases.
Most doctors blamed a germ.
But Joseph Goldberger noticed something strange.
Hospital staff worked beside pellagra patients every day, and they never got sick.
The sick were poor Southerners who lived mostly on cheap corn.
At two orphanages, Goldberger added fresh meat, milk, vegetables and eggs.
Almost all the sick orphans recovered.
Then he fed eleven healthy prisoners mostly corn.
After six months, five of the eleven had pellagra.
Still, the critics refused to believe him.
You see, it's like feeling dizzy when you skip lunch.
No germ did that. An empty plate did.
So in 1916, Goldberger tried to catch pellagra on purpose.
At his so-called filth parties, 16 volunteers took pellagra blood into their bodies.
They felt sick to their stomachs.
But not one of them caught pellagra.
Critics brushed it off anyway, because almost all the volunteers were men.
Goldberger died in 1929, never knowing the missing piece.
In 1937, another scientist found it: a vitamin called niacin.

claims.claim: In 1916 Goldberger injected 16 volunteers, including himself, his wife and his assistant, with pellagric blood; they had diarrhea and nausea but did not get pellagra.
By 1912 South Carolina alone had 30,000 pellagra cases; the epidemic was primarily in the South.
The accepted medical opinion was that pellagra was an infectious disease.
Goldberger noticed hospital staff who worked closely with pellagra patients did not fall sick; cases were overwhelmingly poor Southerners eating corn-based food.
At two orphanages a varied diet with fresh meat, vegetables, milk and eggs led almost all afflicted orphans to recover.
On a corn-based diet, five of eleven healthy prison volunteers got pellagra after six months.
Critics rejected the filth parties for using almost entirely male subjects.
Goldberger died in 1929 and never found the specific nutrient; in 1937 Conrad Elvehjem found pellagra is caused by a lack of niacin.
Pellagra is a disease caused by a lack of the vitamin niacin, with inflamed skin among its symptoms.

cast.goldberger: a 42 year old lean American physician with short wavy dark brown hair, a neat small moustache, deep-set brown eyes and a long serious face, wearing a charcoal three-piece suit, a white wing-collar shirt and a dark tie, 1910s
cast.wife: a 38 year old woman with dark auburn hair pinned up high, a narrow freckled face, a high-collared cream lace blouse and a long navy blue skirt, 1910s
cast.orphan: a 9 year old thin girl with long blond braids, big grey eyes and a faded pink cotton dress with a white collar, 1910s
cast.prisoner: a 27 year old lean prisoner with a tanned face, short dark hair and stubble on his chin, wearing a blue and white striped prison shirt with rolled sleeves, 1910s
cast.critic: a 60 year old stout doctor with a bald head, bushy white side whiskers, small gold pince-nez and a black frock coat with a watch chain, 1910s
cast.chemist: a 36 year old laboratory chemist with thinning blond hair, round black spectacles and a clean-shaven round face, wearing a white lab coat over a dark tie, 1930s
